content.thinking:
I need to write this postmortem using placeholders instead of actual figures. Let me lay out the sequence of events: account page requests started failing, with error rates climbing from a low baseline to a much higher average and spiking at the worst point, sourced from the relevant citation.

Digging deeper, I'm finding the root cause traces to a ZeroDivisionError at a specific line in the spend summary code, tied to the monthly-spend feature flag. The flag logs show evaluations flipping from mostly off to fully on across a narrow window, but the flag provider's change history shows zero recorded changes during that time, and deploy records also show zero changes. This is confusing -- something caused the evaluation split to shift even though no change was logged, so I'm considering whether this was an unrecorded gradual rollout rather than a discrete flag flip, while being careful to only cite figures I can verify.

Tracing the mechanism, the code divides a spend average by this month's purchase count, which is zero for shoppers who haven't purchased yet -- that's the likely trigger once the flag exposed the code path, though this part relies on unverified reading rather than direct measurement. I'm treating the ZeroDivisionError itself as measured fact from the logs, but the explanation for why it happens (zero purchases this month) as an inferred cause, and I'm now thinking through contributing factors like whether a test should have caught this.

I'm identifying gaps in the incident response: the flag rollout wasn't recorded in any change history, so Argus couldn't find a mitigation and refused to act multiple times, and no flag-disable mitigation was ever proposed for it to try. This points toward concrete fixes -- recording flag rollout changes in a change feed, giving the mitigation agent a flag-disable action, adding an error-rate auto-halt during rollouts, and possibly a staged/canary rollout guard given how the warning rate climbed gradually before the failure.

Now I'm being careful about how I cite specifics in my answer -- avoiding exact timestamps and percentages in favor of placeholders like {began} and {alert_raised}, referencing the code location and PR without stating precise figures, and noting the incident closed with just an escalation and an unmerged draft PR rather than a confirmed recovery, so I should phrase the outcome as a lower bound rather than a completed fix.

For the lessons section, I'm noting what went well -- the investigator correctly identified the candidate root cause with solid confidence, and the fix agent drafted a PR quickly -- versus what went wrong, where three investigation rounds each refuted the candidate before it escalated without mitigation while the error kept occurring. I also want to flag the lucky breaks, like the error being scoped to a narrower shopper segment rather than everyone, and note the key assumption that the flag rollout was inferred from evaluation counts since the provider showed no explicit change log explaining how it was enabled.

I'm also being careful with phrasing in the write-up, swapping out specific numbers like "three rounds" for softer language like "repeated rounds" to avoid overly precise figures in the text.

action_items.item: Record every change to a feature flag's exposure (on/off and rollout share) as an event in the production change feed that the Investigator reads, so a flag moving to on appears next to the onset.
Give the Mitigation Agent a reversible action to turn a feature flag off or reduce its exposure, so it can act when the logs show errors starting as the flag's evaluations shift to on.
Tie staged exposure of new flags to the error rate of the pages they affect, so exposure halts automatically when the error rate rises above its baseline.

causal_chain.step: Shoppers who opened their account page got errors. The error rate went from {errors_before} before the onset to {errors_while_broken} on average while broken, and peaked at {errors_at_worst}. The service's own warning lines tracked the same rise, and the paging alert fired.

The failing requests raised ZeroDivisionError in the spend summary code (spend_summary.py). These errors appeared from {began} onward. The earlier account-page errors in the logs were shoppers closing the connection, which is background noise and not the new failure.

The spend summary code started running for account pages because the monthly-spend-feature flag began evaluating as on. Before {began} every evaluation was off. At {began} the evaluations were split between off and on. After that they were on. Argus found no change that explains this. The production change feed showed no deploys or releases in any window it searched, and the flag provider showed no recent flag changes. Neither a deploy nor a recorded flag edit is supported by the record. How the flag came to be on is not shown.

Once that code path ran, it failed for shoppers with no purchase this month. The reading of the code is that the monthly average divides this month's spend by this month's purchase count, which is zero for a shopper who has bought before but not this month. This is a static reading that nothing ran, so it is unverified. It fits the logged error and the error rate rising as the flag moved to full exposure (F1.1). The evidence does not go further than this into why the unguarded division was written or released.

contributing_factors.factor: The change that turned the feature on was not visible in either source Argus checked. The production change feed and the flag provider history both showed no changes. It could only be inferred from flag-evaluation log lines, so the trigger stayed unconfirmed and no mitigation could be proposed.

Argus had no mitigation it could propose for a flag-driven failure. It tried to act, was refused because no mitigation was proposed, and repeated this in later rounds. It then moved to a code fix, so the feature stayed on while a pull request waited for review.

No safeguard was seen that held the feature's exposure back while the error rate rose. The error rate climbed as exposure grew, and the paging rule itself waits {rule_waits} before firing, so a rollout guard tied to the error rate would act sooner than the page.

input.executive_summary: From {began}, a share of shoppers who opened their account page got an error instead of the page. The error rate rose from {errors_before} to {errors_while_broken} on average, and peaked at {errors_at_worst}. Because of that rise, {errors_rise} of traffic failed that would not otherwise have failed. The service was not back to normal when the incident was closed, so it was broken for at least {duration}, and that figure is a lower bound. The failures came from a new account-page feature that crashes for shoppers who have bought before but not this month. Argus found the likely cause but had no mitigation it could propose, so it did not switch the feature off. It escalated with a draft pull request holding a code fix, which was not yet merged when the incident was closed.

got_lucky: The failure, on the code reading, only hits shoppers with no purchase this month, so the error rate stayed well below total failure. This reading is unverified.
went_well: The Investigator pointed at the right cause from the logs, and the Mitigation Agent read the flag provider's history each round. Its candidate named the flag and the failing code location, with confidence {C1.4}.
The Code-Fix Agent produced a draft pull request with a regression test that reproduces the incident's input, and Argus escalated to people with it.
went_wrong: Argus went through several rounds of investigating, trying to mitigate and being refused, and each round re-read the same evidence. The leading candidate was never tried because no mitigation was proposed.
The service was still not back to normal when the incident was closed. The fix was only a draft pull request, and the feature stayed on.

input.root_cause: The spend-summary code behind the monthly-spend-feature flag divides total spend for the current month by the number of purchases in the current month, with no guard for zero. Once the flag was evaluating as on, every shopper with no purchase this month hit ZeroDivisionError and their account page failed. The log shows the error (G5309). That the divisor is zero for such shoppers comes from a static reading of the code that nothing ran, so it is unverified. The evidence does not show why the flag began evaluating as on, because no change was recorded.
input.symptom: Account pages failed for a share of shoppers
